verifyText.value: Dividends & coupon income
Whether you invest in a mutual fund or buy a CD, your investment usually generates investment income.

Mutual funds are professionally managed companies that invest in securities and pass on most of their income to investors who buy shares of the fund. The Securities and Exchange Commission regulates the mutual fund industry. At the end of 2022, mutual funds had combined assets of about $26.964 trillion.

In the case of stocks and mutual funds, income is earned as dividends. Dividends are a distribution of profits. In the case of bonds and savings deposits, income is earned as interest. Interest is an expense that the company is paying to you.
A bond fund invests in bonds that pay interest to the fund manager. The fund manager, in turn, distributes interest to you in the form of dividends.

Interest makes up a type of investment income that is taxed as ordinary income. Dividends make up a type of investment income that is taxed at the same rate as capital gains. Ordinary income includes wages, salaries, and other income that is not capital-gains income. Beginning in 2013, there is also an additional 3.8% tax on net investment income (which includes both interest and dividends) to help fund the Affordable Care Act. The 3.8% tax applies to married filing joint taxpayers with incomes greater than $250,000 and other taxpayers with incomes greater than $200,000.

If you earn more than $1,500 in dividends and interest with a taxable account, the Internal Revenue Service requires you to complete Schedule B of IRS Form 1040. Each institution that pays you dividends or interest is required by law to mail you a Form 1099 by February 1 to help you gather the information necessary to file your income tax return.

If you invest in a taxable account, your dividend and interest income is, naturally, taxable. But if you invest in a tax-deferred account -- an IRA or 401(k) plan for example -- you don't report the income until you begin to take distributions from the account. If you're like most people, you won't begin to take distributions until you reach age 59-1/2. For more information on taking distributions from IRAs, see IRS Pub. 590-B at the IRS Web site.

A common mistake occurs if you reinvest dividends earned on a stock or mutual fund. Reinvesting is a common investing strategy that consists of rolling over investment income into additional shares of the stock or fund.

A common mistake occurs if you reinvest dividends earned on a stock or mutual fund. Reinvesting is a common investing strategy that consists of rolling over investment income into additional shares of the stock or fund.

Investors sometimes think, mistakenly, that they don't have to report reinvested dividends and capital gains as income since they don't handle the money. In fact, they must report reinvested income as income on their tax returns.

For example, say you own 100 shares of Fast-Stride Company. Fast-Stride pays $2 a share in dividends in 2024. Instead of receiving a check, you ask Fast-Stride to reinvest your $200 of dividends in additional shares. If shares are selling for $20 at that time, you increase your investment stake by 10 shares. You would still have to report this $200 as dividend income when you file a return for 2024, even though the money never touches your hands.

A company that helps investors to reinvest their dividends is said to offer a dividend reinvestment plan (DRIP). Mutual funds routinely use a similar automated plan to accommodate investors wishing to reinvest dividends or other income.

In the U.S., dividends are often paid four times a year. Bond interest is usually paid twice a year. In the U.K. and Japan, dividends are usually paid twice a year. The frequency at which you receive dividends and interest -- your investment cash flows -- contributes to the total return you earn on an investment. Total return includes capital gains and any reinvested dividends or interest.
Next, we take a look at capital gains, the other type of income you can receive.

Capital gains

In addition to income you earn from dividends and interest, you can also earn income from capital gains. A capital gain is an increase in the price of an asset over the time that you own it. For example, if you buy a share of stock at $15 and you sell it at $20, your capital gain is $5.
When you file your income tax return, you can add certain expenses such as brokerage fees to calculate the basis of the asset. Increasing the basis allows you to report a smaller capital gain.

For example, if you paid $1 in brokerage fees to buy your $15 share, your basis would be $16. If you sold the share for $20, your capital gain would be $4. For more information on calculating basis, see IRS Pub. 551 at the IRS Web site.
The following calculator can help to calculate the impact of brokerage commissions on your rate of return:

Interest is taxed as ordinary income. Dividends and capital gains, however, may be eligible for a lower tax rate if the gain occurs in a taxable account. (for IRAs, 401(k) plans and other tax-advantaged accounts, capital gains are taxed as ordinary income in the year that you take a distribution from the account.)

Capital gains are classified as either short-term gains or long-term gains. A short-term gain occurs if you have a gain on an asset that you have held for one year or less. The period of time you hold the asset is called the holding period. Short-term capital gains are taxed as ordinary income; they do not qualify for the lower tax rate.
A long-term capital gain occurs if you have a gain on an asset with a holding period of longer than one year.
The following calculator can help to calculate how a holding period of longer than one year affects your after-tax rate of return:

The long-term capital gains tax rate for most investors is 15%. For single taxpayers with taxable income less than $47,025, for married taxpayers filing jointly with taxable income less than $94,055, for married taxpayers filing separately with taxable income less than $47,025, and for head of household taxpayers with taxable income less than $63,000, the long-term capital gains tax rate is 0% in 2024. For single taxpayers with taxable income more than $518,900, for married taxpayers filing jointly with taxable income more than $583,750, for married taxpayers filing separately with taxable income more than $291,850, and for head of household taxpayers with taxable income more than $551,350, the long-term capital gains tax rate is 20% in 2024. Beginning in 2013, there is also an additional 3.8% tax on net investment income (which includes capital gains) to help fund the Affordable Care Act. The 3.8% tax applies to married filing joint taxpayers with incomes greater than $250,000 and other taxpayers with incomes greater than $200,000.

verifyText.value: The wash-sale rule
Investing is a two-edged sword. You may incur a capital loss just as readily as you earn a capital gain.

A capital loss is the opposite of a capital gain: Instead of the price of your shares in a stock or other security increasing over the time you own them, it decreases. Capital losses became a familiar topic with stock investors in 2008 as most of the major stock indexes fell.

Generally, the IRS allows you to deduct capital losses from capital gains and other income. There are limits and rules on when and how much you may deduct. However, investors deprive themselves of using these capital losses to lower taxable income if they sell a stock or other security for a capital loss and buy back the same security too soon afterward.

For example, say you bought 100 shares of a mutual fund a year ago for $10 a share. Shares trade today at $8. You decide to sell all of your shares to record a capital loss of $200 ($2 a share times 100 shares). Since you still like the fund's long-term prospects, you decide to buy back your shares the next day at $8.

It seems like a favorable transaction: You've harvested a $200 capital loss without changing the number of shares you hold in the fund. As you prepare to complete Schedule D of IRS Form 1040, you make plans to deduct these losses from your capital gains and other income.
Under the wash-sale rule, you must wait at least 31 days to buy back the security if you wish to deduct any capital losses. This is a sell-buy example of the wash-sale rule.

The wash-sale rule also applies to buy-sell transactions. For example, if you buy additional shares of the fund to replace shares that you expect to sell, you must wait at least 31 days to sell the old shares if you wish to deduct the capital losses.

If you buy what the IRS considers a substantially identical security -- convertible bonds that can be exchanged for the same shares, for example -- the transaction is also covered under the wash-sale rule.
A consolation of running afoul of the wash-sale rule: You may add the amount of disallowed capital loss to your basis.

Remember your $200 of capital losses? These losses, spread out over 100 shares, equal $2 a share. Adding $2 to your sale price of $8 gives you $10. Your $10 basis is unchanged from your $10 basis on the shares you bought a year ago.
To avoid being tripped up by the wash-sale rule, you should wait at least 31 days to buy the same or a substantially identical security.
Next, we explain the IRS rules for offsetting capital gains with capital losses.
This information should not be interpreted as financial advice. For advice that is specific to your circumstances, you should consult a financial or tax adviser.
Offsetting gains with losses
Capital gains and capital losses represent the profits and losses you earn on your investments when you sell them.

(Note: If you own shares of a mutual fund, the fund will more than likely distribute capital gains to you even if you did not sell any shares. You are required to declare this income as capital gains.)

If your capital losses exceed your capital gains, you may offset all of your capital gains and up to $3,000 of ordinary income. (If you are married and file a separate tax return, the limit on offsetting ordinary income is $1,500.)
Capital losses that exceed the sum of your capital gains and $3,000 of ordinary income may be carried over to next year to offset additional capital gains and ordinary income.

Let's look at an example. For 2023, let's say you had capital gains of $1,000 and capital losses of $6,000. (Ouch.) Since you may offset all of your entire capital gains as well as $3,000 of ordinary income, you use $4,000 of your capital losses for 2023 and carry over $2,000 to 2024.

If you have no capital gains for 2024, you may still offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income. If you incur more capital losses in 2024, you may add these losses to your $3,000 in capital losses. You may offset another $3,000 of ordinary income and carry over the unused balance of capital losses to use in 2025.

Long-term capital gains or losses are earned on capital assets held for longer than one year. Short-term capital gains or losses are incurred on assets held for one year or less. As a result, when you calculate your capital gains and losses, you will have net amounts for long- and short-term assets.

Keep in mind that long-term capital gains are eligible for a lower tax rate but short-term capital gains are taxed as ordinary income (no preferential rate). As a result, long-term gains are more valuable since they cut your tax bill by more. When you offset capital gains with losses, you must first offset any long-term capital gains with long-term capital losses before offsetting short-term capital gains.

For example, let's assume you have $1,000 in both long- and short-term capital gains. You also have $1,500 in long-term capital losses. You must first offset the entire amount of long-term gains before offsetting the $500 of short-term gains.
To help you calculate your capital loss carryover amount, see the worksheet in the instructions for Schedule D of IRS Form 1040.
Next, we explain how to benefit from using tax-advantaged accounts for investing.
This information should not be interpreted as financial advice. For advice that is specific to your circumstances, you should consult a financial or tax adviser.
Tax-advantaged accounts

Whether you invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds or other securities, you keep your investment in an account to keep track of its change in value. Your account of choice is likely to be a tax-advantaged account.

Tax-advantaged accounts are also called tax-favored accounts. These accounts include retirement and college savings accounts. A feature of tax-advantaged accounts is that earnings on your contributions benefit from compounded growth undiminished by taxes.
With tax-deferred accounts, you owe income taxes on the amount you take out (distributions) for the year in which you take it. Tax-deferred accounts include regular IRAs and 401(k) plans.

Other tax-advantaged accounts entitle you to take out all of the money free of taxes if you meet certain requirements. These accounts are funded with contributions that are not deducted from your taxable income. In other words, you pay taxes and then fund the account. These accounts include Roth IRAs, tuition savings plans and education savings accounts.

Let's look at how your savings compounds over time with a tax-advantaged account. The following table shows how large a $10,000 investment in a tax-advantaged account grows to in 10 years. You earn an 8% rate of return and contributions are made at the beginning of each period. To compare the benefits, figures are also shown for taxable accounts where the combined state and federal tax rate is 30%:

As you can see, compounding adds thousands of dollars of additional savings to a tax-advantaged account after 10 years! To get the most from a tax-advantaged account, consider making periodic contributions at the beginning of each period.

Using a tax-advantaged account, however, requires you to think ahead. Make sure you have enough liquidity to make payments (although you're not required to). For example, you probably don't want to funnel money to a retirement account if it means having to scrimp on essential family budget items. You may also find it worthwhile to pay off any unnecessary debt first.

If you take out money early from a tax-advantaged account, you will most likely owe a 10% penalty on the amount you take if you're under age 59 1/2. You will also owe income taxes on the distribution. (There are exceptions to taking money out of a tax-advantaged account early and paying the penalty. These exceptions usually include making a down payment on a first home, paying for educational expenses, or paying for medical bills. You may wish to ask your financial adviser about exceptions for taking money out penalty-free.)

For retirement accounts, the earliest age for taking distributions without being subject to the penalty is generally 59-1/2. For tuition savings plans and education savings accounts, the eligible distribution date is when the account beneficiary -- a child or grandchild, in most cases -- begins to incur school-related expenses.

Taxable accounts
In spite of the benefits of tax-free compounding that tax-advantaged accounts offer, investing with a taxable account likely plays a role in your financial planning.

Consider your checking and savings accounts. More than likely, you use one or both of these accounts daily to transfer funds, pay bills, or withdraw cash. Other reasons for investing with a taxable account include:

Limits on how much you can contribute to most tax-advantaged accounts. Since you may only contribute a certain amount to an IRA or employer-sponsored retirement plan each year, you may have additional savings to invest. These surplus savings are likely to end up in a taxable account.

Tactical asset-allocation considerations. You may choose to leave a lump sum in a taxable money market account or money market fund until a desired investment opportunity comes along. For example, you may wish to invest in a business or real estate. Investing in a tax-advantaged account often narrows your range of investment options.

Type of investments held. If you invest in companies that tend not to pay dividends, you may find that a taxable account isn't such a bad idea. Growth stocks and the funds that invest in growth stocks often don't pay dividends.

Earnings on long-term capital gains -- even those earned on investments in a taxable account -- may qualify for tax rates of 20% or lower. In comparison, earnings on most tax-advantaged accounts are eventually taxed as ordinary income.

If you invest in municipal bonds or muni bond funds, the interest is exempt from federal income taxes. Interest may also be exempt from state income taxes. These tax breaks are available for investments held in a taxable account.

Municipal bonds

Municipal bonds are one way to earn interest income that is usually exempt from federal income taxes. Interest income on muni bonds may also be exempt from state and local income taxes. Generally, you must be a resident of the state or municipality that issues the bonds in order to qualify for this double- or triple tax exemption.

Muni bonds offer predictable interest payments, income-tax exemptions (for most issues), safety and liquidity. According to the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, there were about $3.85 trillion of muni bonds issued and outstanding at the end of the second quarter in 2018. You have to report interest earned on tax-exempt bonds on your tax return but will not owe any taxes if you qualify for the exemptions.

State, city, county, and other local governments sell muni bonds to raise money for specific projects or general operations. These governments usually sell one of two main categories of muni bonds: general obligation bonds or revenue bonds.

General obligation bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the issuing government. That means the bonds have the full weight of the issuing government's taxing authority to ensure repayment. Revenue bonds are repaid from the revenues earned on the specific project that is to be financed from the bond offering.

Whichever type of muni bond you buy, you should find out the issue's credit rating. Web sites of Moody's Investors Service, Standard & Poor's, and Fitch Ratings provide credit ratings for muni bond issues. A good investing rule of thumb is to concentrate on muni issues with an investment-grade rating. Keep in mind that a bond's credit rating should only be a part of your decision to buy a muni bond. You may also wish to check with a financial or tax adviser.

Since tax-exempt muni bonds have built-in tax breaks, their yields are lower than yields of taxable bonds. You can easily compare the yields of tax-exempt and taxable bonds with the taxable-equivalent yield.
Let's say you are thinking of investing in a tax-exempt muni bond issued by an out-of-state municipality that yields 4.0%.

To calculate taxable-equivalent yield of a muni bond, start with your income tax bracket. Let's say you expect your taxable income in 2024 to be $80,000. That puts you in the 22% income tax bracket for most filing statuses. If you subtract your tax bracket from 1.0, you get a reciprocal-of-tax bracket of 0.78.

The second and final step is to divide the 4.0% yield by your reciprocal: 4.0% divided by 0.75 equals a taxable-equivalent yield of 5.13%. This 5.13% yield represents the minimum yield you would need to earn on a taxable bond (with similar risk characteristics) to do better than what the muni bond is offering.

If the bond is issued by your state government, your taxable-equivalent yield increases. A higher taxable-equivalent yield adds to the appeal of the muni bond. For example, if your state income tax rate is 10%, your combined income tax rate is 32% and your reciprocal-of-tax bracket is now 0.68. As a result, your taxable-equivalent yield increases to 5.88%.
Muni bonds are generally sold in denominations of $5,000. Since this amount is more than many small investors can pony up, investing in muni bond funds is one way to gain access to muni bonds.

Muni bond funds invest in muni bonds and sell a proportional interest of the bonds to their fund shareholders. You can find fund data information on muni bond funds at the Web sites of fund data companies Morningstar and Lipper.

Muni bond funds require a smaller initial investment and often allow additional investments of as little as $25 or $50. Like most mutual funds, muni bond funds have automatic reinvestment plans that make it easier to buy additional shares of the fund.

As you can see, muni bonds and muni bond funds offer some attractive tax features that help to boost yields and put them on par with taxable investments. You should keep in mind, however, that financial advisers suggest you don't base your investment decisions primarily on tax considerations. Instead, you may wish to focus on investing in assets that offer a return commensurate with your risk tolerance, investment horizon, and financial goals.

Also keep in mind that, while muni bonds are usually tax-exempt, some muni bonds are taxable. Taxable muni bonds may include those issued to pay for construction of sports stadiums or other projects that do not qualify for federal income tax exemptions.

If you investigate muni bonds and muni bond funds, you're likely to encounter zero-coupon bonds. A zero-coupon bond is a bond that pays no interest. Instead, it is usually sold at a steep discount to par value, often as much as 50% of the bond's face value. For example, a $5,000 zero-coupon bond might sell for $2,500. Prices of zero-coupon bonds bounce around more than the prices of interest-bearing bonds. However, zero-coupon bond yields are higher to compensate for this greater price risk.

As a zero-coupon bond reaches its maturity date, its face value rises towards par value. This price appreciation is treated as imputed interest. The IRS requires you to report imputed interest as taxable income. If you buy zeros that are sold as muni bonds -- a hybrid bond called a zero-coupon muni bond -- you avoid federal income taxes but still must report the imputed interest on your tax return.

Using custodial accounts
A custodial account is an account set up by one party, managed and overseen by another party, and whose assets are intended for the benefit of yet another party.
Custodial accounts are often tax-advantaged accounts. With some tax-advantaged accounts, your contributions are tax-deductible.

With other custodial accounts, the money you take out of the account is exempt from income taxes. In almost all cases, tax-advantaged accounts allow your contributions to grow, or accumulate, tax-free as long as they remain invested in the account.
Custodial accounts are often used to save for college, retirement, or manage your estate. They are also used to gift or transfer assets to children and grandchildren.
Some of the custodial accounts you may use for education planning are qualified tuition plans and Coverdell education savings accounts.

Qualified tuition plans (also called 529 plans) are state-sponsored college savings plans. All states offer these plans, which allow you to contribute to a child's or grandchild's college account. Contributions are income tax-deductible for certain states. For all of these plans, your contributions grow tax-deferred and the earnings are tax-exempt if funds withdrawn from the account are spent on qualified higher education expenses.

Coverdell education savings accounts (formerly called education IRAs) are also a form of a custodial account. You may contribute up to $2,000 per year to an education savings account for each child, grandchild, or other beneficiary. Contributions to education savings accounts begin to phase out at higher incomes.

For single persons, the phase-out begins when modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) reaches $95,000. Allowable contributions phase out completely at $110,000. For married persons filing a joint return, the phase-out limits are exactly twice as much.

The Economic Growth and Tax Relief and Reconciliation Act of 2001 expanded the benefits of qualified tuition plans and education savings accounts. Both of these account types give parents and grandparents greater control over the assets. Qualified tuition plans, in particular, work in the child's favor when applying for college financial aid since the accounts are considered assets of the parents. Note, however, that distributions used for school will count as the student's income in the year following the distribution for financial aid purposes.

The traditional workhorse custodial accounts have been UGMA/UTMA accounts. UGMA/UTMA accounts are taxable accounts that allow you to gift or transfer assets to a minor. They are exempt from the kiddie tax on the first $2,500 of income in 2024. Additional income is taxed at the parent's tax rate. A major drawback of UGMA/UTMA accounts is that the child controls the assets in the account once he or she reaches majority age. (Age 18 in some states and 21 in others.)
Custodial accounts are also used to manage your estate. A trust account allows you to contribute a certain amount to a child, grandchild, or other beneficiary (often, a charitable organization).

The trustee acts as custodian, managing the assets and distributions as you specify when you execute the trust. A trust account is often used for gifting your wealth. For 2024, you may give up to 18,000 a year, tax free, to each beneficiary.
Retirement accounts also have features of custodial accounts, except that you (and a spouse) are the intended beneficiary rather than someone else.
Whether you use a traditional or Roth IRA, or participate in an employer-sponsored retirement plan such as a 401(k) plan, you are essentially opening an account for your own future use.

Tax laws require a custodian to manage a retirement account, even though you can determine how to invest the assets. A bank, brokerage, or other financial institution is frequently the custodian. Traditional IRAs and 401(k) plans allow you to make tax-deductible contributions up to a yearly limit. Earnings grow tax-deferred until you begin to take money out of the account.
With Roth IRAs and Roth 401(k)s, you contribute with after-tax dollars but your earnings are tax-free, provided you have kept the same account open for at least five years.

Except for certain hardships, you have to wait until you turn age 59-1/2 to take money out of these retirement accounts without also paying a 10% penalty. Roth IRAs give you more flexibility, since they don't have required minimum distributions.
